**Short answer:** Res judicata, under the Code of Civil Procedure, prevents a court from trying a suit or issue if the matter directly and substantially in issue has already been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a competent court [S1].

**What the sources say:**
- Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, states that "No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court" [S1].
- The doctrine of res judicata is founded on public policy, aiming for the finality of binding decisions pronounced by competent courts [S5][S6][S7][S8].
- The principle of res judicata is not the foundation of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but rather a statutory recognition of the general principle [S4].
- For Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure to apply, several essential requirements must be met, including that the matter must be directly and substantially in issue in both the former and later suits, and the prior suit must have been between the same parties or persons claiming under them, litigating under the same title [S5].
- The matter in issue must have been heard and finally decided in the first suit [S1][S5].
- The doctrine applies to an issue of fact, an issue of law, or one of mixed law and fact, provided it was decided by a competent court [S7][S8].
- The matter in issue must have been alleged by one party and either denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other in the former suit [S1].
- Any matter that might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in the former suit is deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in that suit [S1].
